claims.text: The onset of premelting in high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles is governed by nanoscale surface segregation.
Preferential migration of lower-melting-point or more mobile elements to the particle surface creates a compositionally heterogeneous surface layer.
The segregated surface layer melts at a lower temperature than the nanoparticle interior.
Controlled annealing, surfactant addition, or atmosphere control can promote or suppress surface segregation.
The governing structural mediator is the degree of surface compositional heterogeneity caused by segregation of lower-melting-point elements.
During thermal treatment, elements with lower intrinsic melting temperatures or higher mobility segregate to the nanoparticle surface.
Surface segregation forms a distinct shell with lower thermal stability than the nanoparticle interior.
The segregated shell initiates premelting below the bulk melting point and thereby dictates the observed nanoparticle melting behavior.
Nanoparticles processed to enhance surface segregation will premelt at lower temperatures than nanoparticles having a more uniform surface composition.
Nanoparticles processed to inhibit segregation will display melting behavior closer to bulk high-entropy-alloy values.
Untreated baseline nanoparticles will have a nearly random bulk and surface elemental distribution.
Untreated baseline nanoparticles will melt at temperatures predicted by bulk-alloy behavior.
The proposed segregation-controlled mechanism should apply to nanoparticles up to approximately 100 nm in size and to high-entropy alloys containing at least five elements.
The mechanism may be less applicable to substantially larger particles.
The mechanism may be less applicable to alloys with fewer components because enthalpic interactions dominate over entropy in those alloys.
The magnitude of the premelting-temperature shift depends on elemental composition, segregation kinetics, and nanoparticle size.
Rapid quenching or related processing conditions can minimize surface segregation.
